Several open-source tools already do this, and they converge on a canonical file that gets written out to each CLI's native format.

- **mcpport** lists, lints, syncs, and converts MCP configs across Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, and Cursor. Its sync is a dry run by default and backs up the target before each write. It also notes that Gemini CLI JSON files with comments are read but never rewritten, to avoid losing them. (List, lint, sync and convert MCP server configs across Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and Cursor.; a JSON target with comments (Gemini CLI allows them) is read but never written, since the rewrite would drop them.)
- **mcp-sync** (EnjoyableWork) keeps one source file at ~/.config/mcp-sync/config.json and writes to Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code, and Codex. (mcp-sync establishes a single local source of truth at ~/.config/mcp-sync/config.json.)
- **mcp-sync** (Rust crate, 1.0.0) syncs a canonical mcp.yaml to Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and others, and can remove servers that are absent from the canonical file. (Sync canonical mcp.yaml to Antigravity, Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and custom targets)
- **sync-agents-settings** pushes Claude Code MCP servers and CLAUDE.md instructions out to Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, and many others. (Sync MCP server configurations and instruction files (CLAUDE.md) from Claude Code to Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Kiro CLI, Cursor, Kimi CLI, Vibe CLI (Mistral), Qwen Code, Amp (Sourcegraph), Cline CLI, Windsurf, and Aider CLI.)

Format differences are the main reason a sync tool is needed. Codex uses TOML, and Codex: TOML under [mcp_servers.<name>], no string interpolation, secrets via env_vars, bearer_token_env_var and env_http_headers. Gemini uses httpUrl (streamable HTTP) or url (SSE), $VAR in env. Config paths are typically ~/.claude.json, ~/.codex/config.toml, and ~/.gemini/settings.json.

One caveat: holstein13/mcp-config-manager lists its Codex config as ~/.codex.json, which doesn't match the ~/.codex/config.toml path the other tools use, so verify that path before relying on it.

I ran one search, so I haven't checked the repos' current maintenance status or licensing.

# mcpport: Summary

**What it is:** A CLI that lists, lints, syncs, and converts MCP server configs across Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, and Cursor.

**Install:** Requires Node 22+.
```
npx mcpport <command>
npm i -g mcpport
```

**Source of truth:** There is no separate canonical file. mcpport reads each agent's own config files, normalizes entries into one shape, and renders them back out in the target agent's format.

**Commands:**
- `npx mcpport list`: shows every server, which agents have it, and whether copies differ. Supports `--agent <id>` and `--json`.
- `npx mcpport lint`: reports errors and warnings. Exits 1 on errors.
- `npx mcpport sync claude cursor`: dry run. Add `--apply` to write.
- `npx mcpport convert <server> --to <agent>`: prints one server in another agent's format. Supports `--out <file>` and `--apply`.

The page does not document an `add` command.

**Config paths:**

| Agent | User config | Project config (`--project <dir>`) |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | `~/.claude.json` (local scope is read-only) | `<dir>/.mcp.json` |
| Codex | `~/.codex/config.toml` | `<dir>/.codex/config.toml` |
| Gemini CLI | `~/.gemini/settings.json` | `<dir>/.gemini/settings.json` |
| Cursor | `~/.cursor/mcp.json` | `<dir>/.cursor/mcp.json` |

**Preserves other settings:**
- JSON files: unrelated keys are kept.
- Codex TOML: comments and unrelated tables are kept.
- Claude Code: rewritten with 2-space indentation, with key order and CRLF line endings kept.
- Gemini JSON files with comments are read but never written, since a rewrite would drop the comments.
- Keys an agent doesn't support are dropped during translation, and mcpport lists what was dropped.

**Dry-run and backup behavior:**
- `list`, `lint`, and `sync` without `--apply` are read-only. `convert` without `--apply` or `--out` only prints.
- Before any write, the target file is copied to `<file>.<timestamp>.bak`.
- Writes go through a temp file and a rename.
- A target that fails to parse is never written.
- Conflicting servers are skipped unless `--force` is given.
- Secret values are redacted in output.

**License:** MIT.

**Last release/commit date:** Not shown on the page. The repo has 14 commits on `main`, and the Releases section is empty.

**Stars:** 0. The repo also shows 0 forks and 0 watchers.

content.content:
## Install

- From a local checkout: `cargo install --path .`
- The page documents only this method.

## Canonical file

- **Name and location:** `mcp.yaml`, read from the current directory by default. Use `--canon <PATH or URL>` to point elsewhere. The page doesn't specify a standard location.
- **Format:** Top-level `version: 1`, an optional `plugins` list, and a `servers` map.

```yaml
version: 1

servers:
  my-server:            # stdio server
    command: npx
    args: ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server"]
    env:
      API_KEY: "${API_KEY}"
    cwd: /path/to/workdir
    enabled: true       # default: true

  remote-server:        # http server
    kind: http
    url: https://mcp.example.com/v1
    headers:
      Authorization: "Bearer ${TOKEN}"
```

## Commands

```bash
mcp-sync sync                          # one-time sync to all targets (default)
mcp-sync watch                         # re-sync on changes
mcp-sync sync --scope global           # global configs only
mcp-sync sync --dry-run --verbose      # preview changes
mcp-sync sync --clean                  # remove servers not in canon
mcp-sync sync --only-target claude     # limit to specific targets
mcp-sync init --output mcp.yaml        # interactive setup
mcp-sync validate --canon mcp.yaml
mcp-sync diff --canon mcp.yaml
mcp-sync completions bash >> ~/.bashrc
```

## Supported targets

- Antigravity (VS Code extension)
- Claude Code
- Codex (OpenAI CLI)
- OpenCode
- Custom targets, loaded as dynamic libraries

**Gemini CLI is not listed.**

## Scope

- **Global (user-level):** Paths vary by OS. Examples: `~/.claude.json` for Claude, `~/.codex/config.toml` for Codex, and `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` for OpenCode on Linux and macOS.
- **Project-level:** `.vscode/mcp.json` (Antigravity), `.mcp.json` (Claude), `.codex/config.toml` (Codex), and `opencode.json` (OpenCode), relative to the project root.
- `--scope` accepts `global`, `project`, or `both` (default `both`). The project root defaults to the auto-detected git root.

## Preserving other settings

The page doesn't say whether unrelated settings in target files are preserved. It only describes syncing the server definitions.

## Dry run and backups

- `--dry-run` prints the changes without writing any files.
- Before modifying a file, the tool creates a timestamped backup alongside it, using a `.bak.<timestamp>` suffix.

## License

MIT

content.content:
**Install**
- **Claude Code plugin:** `claude plugin marketplace add Leoyang183/sync-agents-settings`, then `claude plugin install sync-agents-settings`
- **npx (no install):** `npx sync-agents-settings list`
- **Global:** `npm install -g sync-agents-settings`, then run `sync-agents list`

**Source of truth:** Claude Code is the source. The reader pulls MCP servers from `~/.claude.json` and enabled plugin `.mcp.json` files, then writes them to each target.

**Key commands**
- `sync --dry-run` previews changes; `sync` writes them
- `sync --target gemini` (or codex, opencode, kiro, cursor, and others) syncs one target
- `diff`, `doctor` (drift check), `validate` (schema and capability check), `reconcile --dry-run`
- `sync-instructions` copies CLAUDE.md to other agents' instruction files
- `--report json` gives CI-friendly output

**Config paths (examples)**
- Gemini: `~/.gemini/settings.json`
- Codex: `~/.codex/config.toml`
- OpenCode: `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`
- Kiro: `~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json`
- Cursor: `~/.cursor/mcp.json`
- The page also lists Kimi, Vibe, Qwen, Amp, Cline, and Windsurf paths.

**Preserves other settings?** Partly. The Gemini and OpenCode examples note that "existing settings preserved." The page also says existing servers are never overwritten, so re-running is safe. It does not explicitly state this for every target.

**Dry-run and backup:** `--dry-run` writes no files. By default, affected configs are backed up to `~/.sync-agents-backup/<timestamp>/` before writing. `--no-backup` skips this. Missing target directories are skipped, not created.

**License:** MIT.

**Recent activity:** The page shows 37 commits on `main` and links to the activity tab, but it shows no dated recent changes.

**Stars:** 7 stars, 1 watcher, 1 fork.

The search only partly answers the query. The mcpm.sh GitHub README is the relevant source. It describes MCPM as a tool for managing MCP server installation, configuration, and management across different applications (clients). Its listed supported clients are Claude Desktop (Anthropic), Cursor, and Windsurf. Codex, Gemini CLI, and Claude Code are not named there, so I couldn't confirm from this source that MCPM manages them.

On profiles, the README lists commands such as profile creation, renaming, and removal, and says removing a profile does not delete servers within it. It also describes a Router that lets clients share sessions: The Router also maintains persistent connections to MCP servers, enabling multiple clients to share these server sessions. The README's roadmap lists Server copying/moving (mcpm cp, mcpm mv) and a planned router remote share feature.

The other results cover the native config formats for each client, not MCPM itself. Codex uses TOML [mcp_servers.<name>] tables, and Gemini CLI reads from an mcpServers object in ~/.gemini/settings.json. A Gemini CLI guide also notes that on June 18, 2026, Gemini CLI stopped serving requests for Google AI Pro and Ultra accounts, which may matter if you rely on it.

To confirm whether MCPM supports Codex, Gemini CLI, and Claude Code, check the mcpm.sh documentation or the project's current client list directly.

**`reconcile`, `doctor`, `diff`**

- **`reconcile`**: "One-shot safe reconcile (validate + doctor + sync missing)". It validates, checks drift, and syncs only missing servers.
- **`doctor`**: "Check drift / parse errors between Claude and targets". It reports drift and parse errors. `doctor --fix --dry-run` is described as "Auto-fix from doctor (internally runs reconcile)".
- **`diff`**: "Compare differences" between Claude and the other agents' configs. It's a read-only comparison, and the page doesn't say it writes anything.

**Changed/removed servers and overwrite/prune**

The page documents no `--force` or prune option for MCP sync. It also doesn't say how changed or removed Claude servers are handled. The closest statements are:

- "Existing servers are never overwritten (idempotent, safe to re-run)"
- "Re-running sync will **not overwrite** existing entries (safe to run multiple times)"

The `--on-conflict overwrite|append|skip` flag applies to instruction files in `sync-instructions`, not to MCP sync.

**Codex TOML comments and other tables**

Not stated. The page says only that the Codex writer converts "JSON → TOML" and lists the env sub-table format. It doesn't say whether comments or unrelated tables are preserved. (The "existing settings preserved" examples are for Gemini and OpenCode JSON.)

**Claude scopes read**

The page documents two sources:

- "`~/.claude.json` → `mcpServers` object (user-configured servers)"
- Enabled plugin servers, "matched against `~/.claude/settings.json` `enabledPlugins`"

It doesn't mention local or project scopes.

**Node version**

The page doesn't state a Node version in text. The Node.js badge URL contains `Node.js-%3E%3D18-green`, which decodes to Node.js >=18. This is an inference from the badge.

input.prompt: Does Ruler support global/user-level config (e.g. ~/.config/ruler) and write MCP servers to user-level ~/.claude.json, ~/.codex/config.toml, ~/.gemini/settings.json, or only project-level files? Describe MCP merge vs overwrite behavior, ruler.toml MCP syntax example, install command, and whether it also writes instruction files (AGENTS.md etc) that could clobber things. Stars and latest version.

toolu_01WJY2Zasf9JvmSUw6hhLsQH.prompt: Does Ruler support global/user-level config (e.g. ~/.config/ruler) and write MCP servers to user-level ~/.claude.json, ~/.codex/config.toml, ~/.gemini/settings.json, or only project-level files? Describe MCP merge vs overwrite behavior, ruler.toml MCP syntax example, install command, and whether it also writes instruction files (AGENTS.md etc) that could clobber things. Stars and latest version.

content.content:
**Global config:** Yes. `ruler init --global` creates a config in `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/ruler` (default `~/.config/ruler`), which Ruler uses when no local `.ruler/` directory is found. `--local-only` skips it.

**User-level MCP writes:** No. The page says "Ruler never writes MCP configuration files outside your project root." It does not write to `~/.claude.json`, `~/.codex/config.toml`, or `~/.gemini/settings.json`. It targets project-local files such as `.mcp.json`, `.codex/config.toml`, and `.gemini/settings.json`. For Codex, you must set `CODEX_HOME` to the project's `.codex` directory yourself.

**Merge vs. overwrite:** `merge_strategy` accepts `"merge"` (default) or `"overwrite"`. The CLI flag `--mcp-overwrite` replaces the native MCP config instead of merging. The page doesn't detail exactly how merge treats existing entries. On name conflicts, TOML servers beat legacy JSON servers, and agent-specific servers override global ones with the same name.

**ruler.toml MCP example:**

```toml
[mcp]
enabled = true
merge_strategy = "merge"

[mcp_servers.filesystem]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/path/to/project"]

[mcp_servers.search]
url = "https://mcp.example.com"

[mcp_servers.search.headers]
Authorization = "Bearer your-token"
```

**Install:**
- Global: `npm install -g @intellectronica/ruler`
- One-off: `npx @intellectronica/ruler apply`

Requires Node.js `^20.19.0 || ^22.12.0 || >=23`.

**Instruction files:** Yes, it writes instruction files such as `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, and `.clinerules`, built from `.ruler/*.md`. To limit clobbering:
- Pre-existing non-Ruler files are backed up as `.bak` before replacement. Backups are on by default and can be disabled with `--no-backup`.
- `ruler revert` restores originals from backups or removes generated files.
- Generated files are added to a managed `.gitignore` block by default.
- A root `AGENTS.md` outside `.ruler/` is treated as a source and prepended, so check it before running apply.

**Stars and version:** The repo shows about 3.0k stars. The page doesn't state a latest version number, and its Releases section is empty. The README labels the project a "Beta Research Preview."

content.text:
My recommendation is **mcpport**, a free MIT-licensed CLI that runs locally on Node and needs no account. It's the only tool I found that handles all three of your agents at the user level and makes a point of leaving your other settings alone.

One thing to know up front: mcpport doesn't keep its own master file. It reads each agent's own config, compares them, and copies servers from one agent to the others in the right format. So I'm assuming you'll treat **Claude Code's user config as your one list**. You add servers there and mcpport copies them to Codex and Gemini.

## Why mcpport fits

- **Covers all three:** `~/.claude.json`, `~/.codex/config.toml` (TOML) and `~/.gemini/settings.json`. Cursor too, if you ever need it.
- **Leaves other settings alone:** unrelated JSON keys are kept, and Codex TOML comments and other tables are kept. It won't rewrite a Gemini `settings.json` that contains comments, because that would lose them. If a file can't be parsed, it isn't written.
- **Safe by default:** `sync` only shows what it would do until you add `--apply`. Before writing, it backs up the file to `<file>.<timestamp>.bak` and writes atomically. Servers that conflict are skipped unless you pass `--force`. Secrets are hidden in its output.

**Main caveat:** the project is very new and small, with about 14 commits, 0 stars and no tagged releases. Keep the dry run and backups in your routine for now.

## Install

Requires **Node 22 or newer**. Check with `node -v`.

```bash
npm i -g mcpport        # or run it without installing: npx mcpport <command>
```

## First run

1. **See what you have now.** These two commands only read files:
   ```bash
   mcpport list        # every server, which agents have it, and whether the copies differ
   mcpport lint        # problems in the existing configs
   ```
2. **Make Claude Code the master list.** Add new servers at **user** scope:
   ```bash
   claude mcp add --scope user <name> -- <command> <args...>
   ```
   mcpport treats Claude's default "local" (per-project) scope as read-only, so servers added without `--scope user` won't be copied.
3. **Preview the copy.** I'm assuming the syntax is `sync <from> <to>`, based on the README's `sync claude cursor` example:
   ```bash
   mcpport sync claude codex
   mcpport sync claude gemini
   ```
4. **Write the changes** once the preview looks right:
   ```bash
   mcpport sync claude codex --apply
   mcpport sync claude gemini --apply
   ```
   Only add `--force` when you've changed a server's settings in Claude and want that version to replace the other copies.
5. **Check:** run `mcpport list` again. The servers should show in all three agents with no differences. Your backups sit next to each file as `*.bak`.

After that, adding a server takes three commands: `claude mcp add --scope user …` and then the two `sync … --apply` commands. A small shell alias can run all three.

## Alternatives

- **sync-agents-settings** (`npm i -g sync-agents-settings`, then `sync-agents sync --dry-run`, then `sync-agents sync`). It also uses Claude Code as the source and covers Gemini, Codex and about 10 other agents. It backs up to `~/.sync-agents-backup/`. It has more activity (7 stars, 37 commits), but **it never overwrites servers that already exist**, so later edits to a server won't be copied over. Its docs also don't say whether Codex TOML comments are kept.
- **mcp-sync** (Rust) does keep a real master file (`mcp.yaml`), and supports dry runs, backups and removing servers that aren't in the master. But it **doesn't support Gemini CLI**, and you have to build it from source.
- **Ruler** (about 3k stars) is popular but **only writes project-level** MCP files, never user-level ones. It also generates instruction files like `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`. It doesn't fit what you're after.

I took these details from each project's README and haven't tested the tools myself.

Sources:
- [mcpport](https://github.com/Abdalkaderdev/mcpport)
- [sync-agents-settings](https://github.com/Leoyang183/sync-agents-settings)
- [mcp-sync (Rust) README](https://docs.rs/crate/mcp-sync/latest/source/README.md)
- [mcp-sync (EnjoyableWork)](https://github.com/EnjoyableWork/mcp-sync)
- [mcp-sync on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/mcp-sync/)
- [mcp-config-manager](https://github.com/holstein13/mcp-config-manager)
- [Ruler](https://github.com/intellectronica/ruler)
- [mcpm.sh](https://github.com/lox/mcpm.sh)
- [InventiveHQ: adding MCP servers to AI coding CLIs](https://inventivehq.com/blog/add-mcp-server-to-ai-coding-cli)
